text: We will start with a very simple classification technique called K-Nearest Neighbors.
After this video, you will be able to describe how KNN is used for classification, discuss
the assumption behind KNN, and explain what the K stands for in KNN.
KNN stands for K-Nearest Neighbors.
This is one of the simplest techniques to build a classification model.
The basic idea is to classify a sample based on its neighbors.
So when you get a new sample, as shown by the green circle in the figure, the class
label for that sample is determined by looking at the labels of its neighbors.
KNN relies on the notion of the so-called duck test.
That is, if it looks like a duck, swims like a duck, and quacks like a duck, then it probably
is a duck.
In the classification context, this means that samples with similar input values likely
belong to the same class.
So samples with similar input values should be labeled with the same target label.
This means that classification of a sample is dependent on the target labels of the neighboring
points.
In more detail, then, this is how KNN works.
Given a new sample, look for the samples in the training data that are closest to the
new sample. These are the neighbors. Use the labels of these neighboring points to determine
the label for the new sample. This figure illustrates how KNN works. The problem here
is to determine if a sample should be classified as blue square or red triangle. The green
circle is the new sample. To determine the class label for this new sample, look at its
closest neighbors. These neighbors are the samples within the dashed circle. Two blue
squares and one red triangle. The class labels of the neighboring samples determine the label
for the new sample. The value of k determines the number of nearest neighbors to consider,
so if k equals one, then only the closest neighbor is examined to determine the class
of the new samples, as shown in the left figure. If k equals 2, then the two nearest neighbors
are considered, as seen in the middle figure. If k equals 3, then the three nearest neighbors
are considered, as in the right figure, and so on.
If k equals 1, and only one neighbor is used, then the label for the new sample is simply
the label of the neighbor. This is shown in the left figure. The label of the new sample
is then A, since that is the label of its one nearest neighbor. When multiple neighbors
are considered, then a voting scheme is used. Majority vote is commonly used, so the label
associated with the majority of the neighbors is used as the label of the new sample. This
is what we see in the right figure. With K equals 3, three nearest neighbors are considered.
With two neighbors labeled as A and one as B, the majority vote determines that the new
sample should be labeled as A. In case of a tie, which could be possible if the value
of K is even, then some tie-breaking rule is needed. For example, the label of the closer
neighbor is used or the label is chosen randomly among the neighbors. This is seen in the middle
figure. With two nearest neighbors and each with a different class label, the label for the new
sample is randomly chosen here to be B. With KNN, some measure of similarity is needed to determine
how close two samples are together. This is necessary to determine which samples are the
nearest neighbors. Distance measures such as Euclidean distance are commonly used. Other
Other distance measures that can be used include Manhattan and Hamming distance.
To summarize, KNN is a very simple classification technique.
Note that there is no separate training phase.
There is no separate part where a model is constructed and its parameters adjusted.
This is unlike most other classification algorithms.
KNN can generate complex decision boundaries, allowing for complex classification decisions
to be made. It can be susceptible to noise, however, because classification decisions
are made using only information about a few neighboring points instead of the entire data
set. K and N can be slow, however, since the distance between a new sample and all sample
points in the data must be calculated in order to determine the K nearest neighbors.
